audits.question: Check the located Gobhila naming-rule claim (2.8.8-17) or the entry's shiksha six-concern passage against the named school/edition: distinguish textual rule, translator's terminology and universal ancient practice.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/india-vedic.md:165 — section 'Naming practices: genealogy, attribution, and occasion', bullet 'Gṛhya naming-rite prescriptions belong to another textual genre and vary by school: the Gobhila tradition…', citing Gobhila Gṛhya Sūtra 2.8.8–17 in Oldenberg, SBE 30, with the entry's link to https://sacred-texts.com/hin/sbe30/sbe30020.htm
audits.entry_claim: The Gobhila tradition gives the name at ten nights or later, prescribing for boys a name beginning with a sonant, containing a semivowel, ending in a long vowel or the visarga (with a kṛt suffix), and for girls an odd-syllable name ending in -dā, with offerings to the child's tithi and nakshatra (Gobhila Gṛhya Sūtra 2.8.8–17, in Oldenberg, SBE 30); Oldenberg's notes cross-reference the parallels (Śāṅkhāyana 1.24, Āśvalāyana 1.15, Pāraskara 1.17); the entry bounds the rule: 'Apply any such rule only with its school and passage.'
audits.source_citation: Hermann Oldenberg, trans., The Grihya Sutras, Part 2 (SBE30), Sacred Books of the East vol. 30, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1892, 'Grihya Sutra of Gobhila: II, 8' (Kâṇḍikâ 8), §§ 8, 12, 14–16, and translator's footnotes to §§ 8, 12, 14
audits.source_locator: Gobhila Gṛhya Sūtra II,8.8 (namadheyakarana when ten nights, a hundred nights, or one year have elapsed); II,8.12 (sacrifice to Pragâpati, to the birth Tithi, to the birth Nakshatra, and to their presiding deity); II,8.14 (name beginning with a sonant, with a semivowel in it, with a long vowel or the Visarga at the end, formed with a Krit suffix); II,8.15 (no Taddhita suffix); II,8.16 (odd number of syllables, ending in -dâ, to girls); footnote to §14 ('Sâṅkhâyana-Grihya I, 24, 4; Âsvalâyana I, 15, 4; Pâraskara I, 17, 2. In the text read dîrghâbhinishtânântam instead of dîrghâbhinishthânântam.')
audits.source_excerpt: he should give him a name beginning with a sonant, with a semivowel in it, with a long vowel or the Visarga at the end, (and formed with) a Krit (suffix).
audits.retrieval_method: FetchURL of the Wayback Machine snapshot of the entry's cited sacred-texts.com SBE30 chapter page, after the direct sacred-texts fetch returned HTTP 403; the full Kâṇḍikâ 8 chapter text with footnotes was retrieved, not a search snippet. Evidence copy: reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/round6-13/gobhila-sbe30-2-8-retrieval.md
audits.basis: This is the named school/edition translation the entry itself cites (Oldenberg, SBE 30, Gobhila II,8), so the retrieved English sūtras directly test each element of the entry's paraphrase, including the claimed parallel-school footnotes and the school-bounded framing.
audits.coupling_implication: Naming rules are school-specific gṛhya prescriptions, not a pan-Vedic or universal ancient convention: a fictional naming system should attach each rule to a named school and passage, and keep boy-rule (II,8.14–15), girl-rule (II,8.16), timing (II,8.8) and birth-tithi/nakshatra offerings (II,8.12, 20) as separate couplable slots. 'Sonant', 'semivowel', 'Krit', '-dâ' are the translator's grammar labels for a Sanskrit rule — mediation, not a universal design constraint.
audits.limits: Translation-mediated: English inspected, underlying Sanskrit not inspected this pass. Oldenberg's rendering rests on at least one conjectural emendation (footnote to §14) and supplies parenthetical grammatical glosses; the Sanskrit forms behind 'sonant/semivowel/Krit/-dâ' were not independently checked. The entry's 'ten nights or later' compresses the text's three named timings (10 nights, 100 nights, one year). The sacred-texts page was retrieved via a Wayback snapshot whose exact capture timestamp was not displayed in the extracted text; snapshot-vs-live identity rests on the retrieved chapter matching the cited SBE 30 pagination and title. A domestic-rule text of one school establishes no universal ancient practice, and the footnotes themselves record inter-school variance. Verdict is author-side evidence, not independent promotion verification.

additional_excerpts.II,8.8: When ten nights have elapsed after (the child's) birth, or a hundred nights, or one year, the Nâmadheyakarana (or giving a name to the child, is performed).
additional_excerpts.II,8.12: He then sacrifices to Pragâpati, to the Tithi (of the child's birth), to the Nakshatra (of the child's birth), and to the (presiding) deity (of that Tithi and of that Nakshatra).
additional_excerpts.II,8.16: (He should give a name with) an odd (number of syllables), ending in -dâ, to girls.
additional_excerpts.footnote_to_II,8.14: Sâṅkhâyana-Grihya I, 24, 4; Âsvalâyana I, 15, 4; Pâraskara I, 17, 2. In the text read dîrghâbhinishtânântam instead of dîrghâbhinishthânântam.

audits.questions_for_parent: Whether the entry's 'ten nights or later' should be tightened in a future round to the three named timings (10 nights, 100 nights, one year); whether a Sanskrit edition (e.g. GRETIL) should confirm §14 independently of Oldenberg's emendation.

audits.question: Check the Satapatha consecration black-antelope skin/horn or cloth passage: distinguish sitting surfaces versus worn garment and school-specific prescription versus a pan-Vedic costume reconstruction.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/india-vedic.md:127 — table row 'Black-antelope skins as consecration ground | 3.2.1.1–9 | Skin joins worlds; the consecrated becomes an embryo entering metres | These passages describe sitting surfaces: do not automatically draw them as a worn cloak' — and :130 — row 'Attached antelope horn | 3.2.1.18, 28–31 | Womb analogy; prescribed scratching implement | Attachment differs between Mādhyandina and Kāṇva witnesses noted by Eggeling' — section 'Fire-ritual dress: consecration creates a temporary person', whose witness links are at :120
audits.entry_claim: Soma-sacrifice dīkṣā evidence from the Mādhyandina Śatapatha (E85), not uniform dress for every fire rite or every Vedic person: black-antelope skins as consecration ground (3.2.1.1–9) couple skin and worlds, with the consecrated as embryo entering metres, and these passages describe sitting surfaces rather than a worn cloak; the attached antelope horn (3.2.1.18, 28–31) carries the womb analogy and serves as the prescribed scratching implement, with attachment differing between Mādhyandina and Kāṇva witnesses as noted by Eggeling.
audits.source_citation: Julius Eggeling, trans., The Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa According to the Text of the Mādhyandina School, Part II (Books III–IV), Sacred Books of the East vol. 26, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1885, Kāṇḍa III, Adhyāya 2, Brāhmaṇa 1, §§ 1–9, 18, 28–31, with translator's footnotes 3 and 9 (wisdomlib hosting of the entry's cited chapter page)
audits.source_locator: ŚB (Mādhyandina) III,2,1,1 — two skins spread on the ground as image of the two worlds; §3 — one skin as three worlds, white/black assignment 'or, if he likes, conversely'; §5 — squats behind the skins, touching where white and black hair join; §6 — consecrated becomes embryo, enters the metres; §8 — kneels with right knee on the skin (carman/śarman play); §9 — 'He must indeed sit down first on the hind part (of the skin)'; §18 — ties a black deer's horn to the end of the garment; §28 — horn = womb, bound tightly to the garment end; §29 — open part upward like a womb bearing an embryo; §31 — scratching only with the horn; footnote 9 — Mādhyandina: thrum (daśā) of the nether garment, Kāṇva: hem of the upper garment
audits.source_excerpt: South of the Āhavanīya he spreads two black antelope skins on the ground, with the neck parts towards the east: thereon he consecrates him. … He must indeed sit down first on the hind part (of the skin).
audits.retrieval_method: FetchURL of the entry's own cited wisdomlib chapter page (Eggeling translation, ŚB Kāṇḍa III, Adhyāya 2, Brāhmaṇa 1); full chapter §§ 1–40 with footnotes retrieved, not a search snippet. Evidence copy: reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/round6-13/satapatha-3-2-1-retrieval.md
audits.basis: The entry names this exact chapter (3.2.1) and links this page as its primary English witness; the retrieved text confirms the spread-on-ground and sitting/kneeling verb set for §§ 1–9, the world and embryo/metres couplings, the horn's garment-end attachment and womb analogy for §§ 18, 28–31, and the Mādhyandina/Kāṇva difference recorded in footnote 9.
audits.coupling_implication: Consecration dress couplings stay procedural and school-bounded: in Mādhyandina ŚB 3.2.1.1–9 the skins are a sitting surface on the ground joining worlds, while the horn is a worn garment-end attachment with a womb analogy and a scratching function. A fictional rite can model 'surface vs worn item' as distinct slots — spread skins, hempen zone, head wrap, attached horn — instead of reading one cloak from the whole sequence, and can let two textual schools attach the same implement to different garments.
audits.limits: English translation only (Eggeling 1885, colonial-era terminology and editorial reconstructions; e.g. 'black deer's horn' for the kṛṣṇājina implement); wisdomlib hosting and its page framing are mediators. The Sanskrit text and the Kāṇva recension were not independently inspected this pass — the Mādhyandina/Kāṇva attachment difference is accepted as reported in Eggeling's footnote 9. The sitting-surface confirmation covers 3.2.1.1–9 exactly as the entry scopes it; §18 does attach the horn to a garment end, and the entry's own horn row keeps that distinction. This is one school's Soma-sacrifice dīkṣā prescription, supporting no pan-Vedic costume reconstruction. Verdict is author-side evidence, not independent promotion verification.

additional_excerpts.III,2,1,3: Those (hairs) which are white are an image of the sky; those which are black are (an image) of this (earth);--or, if he likes, conversely: those which are black are an image of the sky, and those which are white are (an image) of this (earth).
additional_excerpts.III,2,1,6: Now, he who is consecrated becomes an embryo, and enters into the metres: hence he has his hands closed, since embryos have their hands closed.
additional_excerpts.III,2,1,18: Thereupon he ties a black deer's horn to the end (of his garment).
additional_excerpts.III,2,1,28: the black deer skin is the same as that sacrifice, and the black deer's horn is the same as that womb
additional_excerpts.III,2,1,31: therefore the consecrated should scratch himself with the black deer's horn and with nothing but the black deer's horn
additional_excerpts.footnote_9: The Mādhyandinas tied the horn to the unwoven end (thrum, daśā) of the nether garment which was tucked through (par. 13) and then allowed to hang down in front. The Kāṇvas, on the other hand, tied it to the hem of the upper garment (uttarasice! Kāṇva text); cf. Kāty. VII, 3, 29 scholl.

audits.questions_for_parent: Whether a future round should inspect the Kāṇva Sanskrit (or Kātyāyana-Śrautasūtra VII,3,29 commentary) to confirm footnote 9's attachment difference first-hand rather than through Eggeling's footnote; the entry's ŚB 3.2.1 wisdomlib link and this audit's copy are the retrieval record.
